q: How robust are proGenomes3/pg4 species-cluster boundaries relative to GTDB and NCBI-taxonomy discordance, and how well do they cover rare taxa (singleton clusters, environmental novelty) that have no independent species designation?
basis: Replication showed 54.2% (17,810/32,887) of pg4 ANI clusters are singletons, and 10% of clusters (3,285/32,887) lack any GTDB consensus label. Slice-100 genus agreement with NCBI was 71.4% and species agreement only 42.9%; many mismatches are known GTDB reclassifications (e.g. Brucella tianjinense = Falsochrobactrum tianjinense). The paper claims consistency 'within pg', not agreement with either NCBI or GTDB — but the practical question of when a pg cluster should be trusted as a species remains open, especially in the singleton / no-GTDB-consensus tail where independent labels do not exist.
next_steps: Cross-map every pg4 ANI cluster to the latest GTDB (R220+) and NCBI taxonomy releases; quantify what fraction split, merge, or reclassify per release.
For the 3,285 GTDB-consensus-missing clusters, run a placement pipeline (e.g. GTDB-Tk classify_wf) and see how many receive stable placements vs remain novel.

Compute intra-cluster ANI mean/variance and inter-cluster nearest-neighbor ANI to characterize cluster tightness across the singleton vs polytype spectrum; flag clusters where ANI cohesion is <95% or nearest-neighbor overlap exceeds 5%.
Compare pg4 species boundaries against dRep and skani re-clustering on the same reps to test methodological sensitivity.

q: Does proGenomes3/pg4 integrate metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) alongside isolate genomes, and if so, does the paper's annotation-quality claim hold uniformly across those two provenance classes — or does MAG inclusion introduce systematic drift that biases downstream ecology and functional-inference?
basis: Replication observed a very heterogeneous N50 distribution (min 12.9 kb, median 351 kb, mean 1.27 Mb, max 7.09 Mb) and 41% of the slice was still at Contig-level assembly, with only 23% Complete Genomes. This is consistent with accepting fragmented drafts (potentially MAG-derived), but the replication did not stratify QC-pass rates or CheckM/GUNC statistics by isolate vs MAG provenance. The paper's uniform 'high-quality' framing may mask systematically lower biological completeness / higher contamination in the MAG subset that would bias any downstream community-composition or functional-abundance analysis.
next_steps: Join pg4_ncbi_taxonomy against NCBI's assembly_source and refseq_category fields to segregate isolate vs MAG accessions.
Re-run the 79.3% CheckM pass rate calculation separately for the two provenance classes; test whether MAG reps disproportionately populate the failure tail.
Repeat the GUNC clade-separation-score analysis stratified by provenance to detect MAG-specific chimerism.
Compare downstream eggNOG COG-category distributions on isolate reps vs MAG reps in matched species clusters to quantify functional-annotation drift.

q: How sensitive is pg4's pan-genome-scale gene family definition (via eggNOG-mapper on representatives) to alternative clustering thresholds (mmseqs2 easy-cluster identity/coverage, CD-HIT thresholds), and does the paper's 'consistent functional annotation' claim survive threshold perturbation across the eggNOG/KEGG/Pfam cross-database landscape?
basis: Claim C6 (consistent functional annotation via eggNOG-mapper) was explicitly skipped in the replication as out-of-budget (1.5 GB eggNOG-representatives file). This is one of the paper's four headline consistency claims, and it went untested — leaving a genuine open question about whether gene-family calls are stable under standard alternative clustering parameterizations that other pan-genome studies routinely use.
next_steps: Download pg4's eggNOG-representatives artifact; re-run eggNOG-mapper v2.1.x on a stratified 500-rep sample and compare COG/KEGG/Pfam calls to the shipped annotations.

Independently cluster the same rep proteomes with mmseqs2 easy-cluster at (0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90) identity thresholds and CD-HIT at (0.40, 0.70, 0.90); measure family-count deltas and per-family membership Jaccard.
Quantify cross-database concordance (eggNOG vs KEGG vs Pfam) on a common test set; report fraction of families whose top annotation flips under threshold change.
Publish a sensitivity table so downstream users can pick a threshold defensibly.

q: How well do proGenomes3/pg4 annotations serve large-scale AMR-gene, virulence-factor, and secondary-metabolite BGC surveys — and what are the false-positive and false-negative rates compared to specialized databases (CARD, VFDB, MIBiG/antiSMASH)?
basis: The paper foregrounds pg3 as a substrate for downstream mining (AMR, virulence, BGCs) but the replication did not touch any of these downstream applications. The 97% highly-important-strain retention rate is encouraging for known-model coverage, but says nothing about recall/precision of the specialized annotation layers that most consumers of pg would actually use.
next_steps: Run CARD-RGI on a random 500-rep sample from pg4 and compare AMR-gene calls against pg4's shipped AMR annotations (precision, recall, F1 per drug class).
Do the same for VFDB (virulence factors) and antiSMASH+MIBiG (BGCs).
Stratify errors by phylum and by isolate/MAG provenance to see if any group is systematically under- or over-annotated.
For BGCs specifically, compare cluster-boundary calls (start/end coordinates) not just presence/absence, since downstream chemistry inference is boundary-sensitive.

q: What is proGenomes3/pg4's actual update cadence and versioning discipline, and how does it compare to GTDB's release cycle for the purpose of reproducible longitudinal microbiome or genome-mining analyses?
basis: The replication documented a silent, undocumented v3->v4 backend swap: the paper's cited URL still hosts a page listing 'proGenomes3_*' filenames that now return HTTP 404, while only 'pg4_*' files are actually served. Users following the paper get 404s with no version banner. This is a real reproducibility hazard for anyone attempting a longitudinal study — you cannot pin an analysis to 'proGenomes3 as of the paper' from the paper's own URL today. GTDB, in contrast, publishes explicit R220/R221/etc. releases with permanent download URLs. Whether pg's practice can support versioned science is an open question with community-level implications.
next_steps: Audit progenomes.embl.de for any historical snapshots, DOI'd Zenodo mirrors, or version manifests; email the Bork group asking whether v3 tarballs can be reposted or DOI-minted.
Compare pg's file naming, changelog presence, and per-release DOI practice against GTDB, RefSeq, and BV-BRC on a documented scorecard.

Propose a minimal versioning contract to the pg maintainers (e.g. permanent per-release subdirectories, a machine-readable manifest, a top-of-page version banner, and DOI minting) and check whether the group adopts it.
In the interim, wrap pg4 downloads with a hash-pinned manifest so downstream analyses can at least detect silent backend swaps in their own pipelines.
